source_text: OBLATRANTEM te et adversus Deum, qui unus et verus est, ore sacrilego et verbis impiis obstrepentem frequenter, Demetriane, contempseram, verecundius ac melius existimans errantis imperitiam silentio spernere, quam loquendo dementis insaniam provocare. Nec hoc sine magisterii divini auctoritate faciebam, cum scriptum sit: In aures imprudentis noli quicquam dicere, ne, quando audierit, irrideat sensatos sermones tuos. Et iterum: Noli respondere imprudenti ad imprudentiam ejus, ne similis fias illi. Et sanctum quoque jubeamur intra conscientiam nostram tenere, nec inculcandum porcis et canibus exponere, loquente Domino et dicente: Ne dederitis sanctum canibus, neque miseritis margaritas vestras ante porcos, ne inculcent eas pedibus, et conversi elidant vos. Nam, cum ad me saepe, studio magis contradicendi quam voto discendi, venires, et, clamosis vocibus personans, malles tua impudenter ingerere quam nostra patienter audire, ineptum videbatur congredi tecum, quando facilius esset et levius turbulenti maris concitos fluctus clamoribus retundere quam tuam rabiem tractatibus coercere. Certe et labor irritus et nullus effectus, offerre lumen caeco, sermonem surdo, sapientiam bruto; cum nec sentire brutus possit, nec caecus lumen admittere, nec surdus audire. Haec considerans, saepe conticui, et impatientem patientia vici, cum nec docere indocilem possem, nec impium religione comprimere, nec furentem lenitate cohibere. Sed enim, cum dicas plurimos conqueri quod bella crebrius surgant, quod lues, quod fames saeviant, quodque imbres et pluvias serena longa suspendant nobis imputari, tacere ultra non oportet; ne jam non verecundiae sed diffidentiae esse incipiat quod tacemus, et dum criminationes falsas contemnimus refutare, videamur crimen agnoscere. Respondeo igitur et tibi, Demetriane, pariter et caeteris quos tu forsitan concitasti, et adversum nos odia tuis maledicis vocibus seminando, comites tibi plures radicis atque originis tuae pullulatione fecisti; quos tamen sermonis nostri admittere credo rationem: nam qui ad malum motus est mendacio fallente, multo magis ad bonum movebitur veritate cogente. Dixisti per nos fieri et quod nobis debeant imputari omnia ista quibus nunc mundus quatitur et urgetur, quod dii vestri a nobis non colantur. Qua in parte, quia ignarus divinae cognitionis et veritatis alienus es, illud primo in loco scire debes, senuisse jam mundum, non illis viribus stare quibus prius steterat, nec vigore et robore eo valere quo antea praevalebat. Hoc etiam, nobis tacentibus et nulla de Scripturis sanctis praedicationibusque divinis documenta promentibus, mundus ipse jam loquitur et occasum sui rerum labentium probatione testatur. Non hyeme nutriendis seminibus tanta imbrium copia est, non frugibus aestate torrendis solis tanta flagrantia est, nec sic vernante temperie sata laeta sunt, nec adeo arboreis foetibus autumna foecunda sunt. Minus de effossis et fatigatis montibus eruuntur marmorum crustae, minus argenti et auri opes suggerunt exhausta jam metalla, et pauperes venae breviantur in dies singulos et decrescunt, deficit in arvis agricola, in mari nauta, miles in castris, innocentia in foro, justitia in judicio, in amicitiis concordia, in artibus peritia, in moribus disciplina. Putasne tantam posse substantiam rei senescentis existere quantum prius potuit novellu adhuc et vegeta juventa pollere? Minuatur necesse est quicquid fine jam proximo in occidua et extrema devergit. Sic sol in occasu suo radios minus claro et igneo splendore jaculatur; sic, declinante jam cursu, exoletis cornibus luna tenuatur, et arbor quae fuerat ante viridis et fertilis, arescentibus ramis fit postmodum sterili senectute deformis; et fons qui, exundantibus prius venis, largiter profluebat, senectute deficiens, vix modico sudore distillat. Haec sententia mundo data est, haec Dei lex est, ut omnia orta occidant et aucta senescant, et infirmentur fortia, et magna minuantur, et cum infirmata et diminuta fuerint, finiantur. Christianis imputas quod minuantur singula, mundo senescente. Quid si et senes imputent Christianis quod minus valeant in senectute, quod non perinde ut prius vigeant auditu aurium, cursu pedum, oculorum acie, virium robore, succo viscerum, mole membrorum; et cum olim ultra octingentos et nongentos annos vita hominum longaeva procederet, vix nunc possit ad centenarium numerum perveniri? Canos videmus in pueris, capilli deficiunt antequam crescant; nec aetas in senectute desinit, sed incipit a senectute. Sic in ortu adhuc suo ad finem nativitas properat; sic quodcumque nunc nascitur, mundi ipsius senectute degenerat: ut nemo mirari debeat singula in mundo coepisse deficere, quando totus ipse jam mundus in defectione sit et in fine.
pass_a_gloss: I had frequently despised you, Demetrianus, who with sacrilegious mouth and impious words were often speaking against God, who is one and true, thinking it more reverent and better to scorn the ignorance of the erring in silence, rather than to provoke the madness of the demented by speaking. And I was not doing this without the authority of divine teaching, since it is written: Do not say anything in the ears of the imprudent, lest, when he hears, he ridicules your sensible words. And again: Do not respond to the imprudent according to his imprudence, lest you become like him. We are also commanded to keep the holy within our conscience, and not to cast pearls before swine and dogs, speaking and saying: Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to tear you apart. For when you often came to me, more with the intention of contradicting than of learning, and, with loud voices, preferred to impudently impose your own rather than patiently listen to ours, it seemed foolish to engage with you, since it would be easier and less troublesome to calm the turbulent waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your rage with discussions. Certainly, it is a labor in vain and without effect to offer light to the blind, speech to the deaf, wisdom to the brute; since the brute cannot feel, the blind cannot admit light, and the deaf cannot hear. Considering these things, I often kept silent, and overcame the impatient with patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious with religion, nor calm the raging with gentleness. But since you say that many complain that wars arise more frequently, that plagues, that famines rage, that rains and showers suspend the long periods of fair weather for us, it is not fitting to remain silent any longer; lest what we keep silent about begin not to be out of reverence but out of diffidence, and while we disdain to refute false accusations, we seem to acknowledge the crime. I respond, therefore, to you, Demetrianus, and equally to the others whom you may have stirred up, and who, with your slanderous voices, have sown hatred against us, and have made many companions for yourself from the root and origin of your own multitude; whom, however, I believe will admit the reason of our words: for he who is moved to evil by the deceit of falsehood, will be moved much more to good by the compulsion of truth. You said that through us these things happen, and that all these things, by which the world is now shaken and pressed, should be imputed to us, because your gods are not worshiped by us. In this part, since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and alien to truth, you should first know that the world has already grown old, does not stand with those powers with which it previously stood, nor is it strong with the same vigor and robustness with which it previously prevailed. This also, even if we were silent and did not bring forth any documents from the holy Scriptures and divine preachings, the world itself now speaks and testifies to its own decline with the proof of its failing things. There is not such an abundance of rains to nourish the seeds in winter, not such a burning of the sun to dry the fruits in summer, nor are the sown things so joyful in the spring, nor is autumn so fertile with the fruits of the trees. Less and less marble is extracted from the excavated and exhausted mountains, less and less wealth of silver and gold is produced, since the metals are now exhausted, and the poor veins are shortened day by day and decrease, the farmer fails in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp, innocence in the forum, justice in judgment, concord in friendships, skill in arts, discipline in morals. Do you think that such a great substance of a thing that is growing old can exist as it was able to when it was still new and in its vigorous youth? It is necessary that whatever is already near its end and is declining into its final stages must decrease. Thus, the sun, in its setting, throws its rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus, with its course already declining, the moon is diminished with its worn-out horns; and the tree, which was previously green and fertile, becomes sterile and deformed in its old age, with its withering branches; and the spring, which previously flowed abundantly, with its veins now failing in old age, barely drips with a small trickle. This sentence has been given to the world, this is the law of God, that all things that have arisen will decline, and all things that have grown will grow old, and the strong will be weakened, and the great will be diminished, and when they have been weakened and diminished, they will come to an end. You impute to Christians that individual things are decreasing, with the world growing old. What if the old also impute to Christians that they are less strong in old age, that they do not thrive as much as before in hearing, in the running of feet, in the sharpness of eyes, in the robustness of strength, in the moisture of viscera, in the mass of limbs; and since human life previously lasted for eight hundred or nine hundred years, it can now hardly reach the number of a hundred? We see gray hair in children, hair is lacking before it grows; nor does age end in old age, but begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, nativity hastens to its end; thus, whatever is now born, degenerates with the old age of the world itself: so that no one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

pass_b_english: I had long held you in contempt, Demetrius, because with sacrilegious mouth and impious words you frequently railed against the one true God. I thought it more reverent and better to pass over the ignorance of a wanderer in silence than to provoke a madman’s insanity by speaking. And I did not act without divine authority, since it is written: “Do not speak in the ears of a fool, lest he despise the wisdom of your words” (Prov. 9:7–8). And again: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, or you will be like him yourself” (Prov. 9:7–8). We are also commanded to keep what is holy within our own conscience and not to throw pearls before swine and dogs, for the Lord said: “Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you” (Matt. 7:6). For you often came to me more intent on contradicting than on learning, and with loud clamor you chose to force your own views on me rather than listen patiently to mine. It seemed pointless to engage you, because it would be easier to calm the raging waves of a stormy sea with shouts than to restrain your fury with reason. To offer light to the blind, speech to the deaf, wisdom to a brute beast is labor in vain and without effect; a beast cannot perceive, a blind man cannot receive light, a deaf man cannot hear. Weighing this, I often kept silent and overcame your impatience with my patience, since I could neither teach the unteachable, nor restrain the impious by religion, nor calm the raging by gentleness.

But now you claim that many complain that wars break out more frequently, that plagues and famines rage, and that the long fair weather has given way to rains and showers — and that all this is to be laid at our door because your gods are not worshiped by us. If I stayed silent any longer it would look not like reverence but like fear, and by refusing to refute false accusations we would seem to admit the charge. So I answer you, Demetrius, and equally the others you may have stirred up, who with your slanderous voices have sown hatred against us and gathered many companions from the root and stock of your own kind. Yet I believe they will accept the reason of our words: whoever is driven to evil by the deceit of falsehood will be driven much more to good by the compulsion of truth.

You say these disasters happen through us and must be imputed to us because your gods are not worshiped by us. On this point, since you are ignorant of divine knowledge and a stranger to the truth, you must first understand that the world has grown old. It no longer stands with the powers it once had, nor does it prevail with the vigor and strength it formerly possessed. Even if we kept silent and produced no testimonies from the holy Scriptures or divine preaching, the world itself now speaks and testifies to its own decline by the evidence of failing things. The winter rains are no longer so abundant to nourish the seed; the summer sun no longer burns so fiercely to ripen the fruit; spring crops are no longer so joyful, autumn no longer so fruitful with the produce of the trees. Less and less marble is quarried from the excavated and exhausted mountains; less and less silver and gold is yielded by mines now drained; the poor veins shrink day by day and dwindle. The farmer fails in the fields, the sailor on the sea, the soldier in the camp; innocence fails in the forum, justice in the courts, concord in friendships, skill in the arts, discipline in morals.

Do you think a thing that is aging can still possess the substance it had when it was new and in vigorous youth? Whatever is already near its end and declining into its final stages must necessarily diminish. Thus the sun at its setting casts rays with less clear and fiery splendor; thus the moon, its course declining, wanes with worn-out horns; and a tree once green and fertile becomes sterile and deformed by withered branches in sterile old age. A spring that once flowed abundantly from overflowing veins, failing with age, barely drips a thin trickle. This sentence has been passed on the world; this is the law of God: that all things that arise will decline, all that grow will grow old, the strong will be weakened, the great diminished, and when weakened and diminished they will come to an end.

You blame Christians because individual things decrease while the world grows old. What if the elderly also blamed Christians because they are less strong in old age — because they do not thrive as before in hearing, in running, in sharpness of sight, in robustness of strength, in the moisture of their viscera, in the mass of their limbs? Human life once lasted eight or nine hundred years; now it can hardly reach a hundred. We see gray hair in children; hair falls out before it grows. Age does not end in old age; it begins with old age. Thus, in its very birth, nativity hastens toward its end; thus whatever is now born degenerates with the old age of the world itself. No one should wonder that individual things in the world have begun to fail, when the whole world itself is already in decline and at its end.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation. Pass B provides a polished version that correctly identifies and expands the inline scripture citations (Proverbs 9:7-8 and Matthew 7:6) which were present in the Latin as allusions. The title 'Response to Demetrianus' correctly names the thought/subject of the address.
